overview: The Icelandic Commonwealth was a society of farms, chieftains and assemblies, without a resident king. Its Alþingi began in 930. The atlas shows only 1000-1200 of this longer history. Laws, farm buildings and books reveal both practical work and a strong tradition of preserving words.

periods.title: Assembly and remembered law
periods.summary: The Alþingi met at Þingvellir, where laws were spoken aloud.

periods.title: Writing and contested authority
periods.summary: Law began to be written down in 1117-18; manuscripts and farm remains illuminate the Commonwealth's later centuries.

periods.title: Agreement with Norway
periods.summary: Icelanders accepted the Norwegian king through agreements made across 1262-64.

items.text: The law speaker recited the laws over a three-year cycle and repeated the procedural rules each summer. Remembering and speaking clearly were important public skills. This was not the same as every household having a printed legal handbook.

Þingvellir's assembly heard announcements and legal business as well as speeches. Its present landscape should not be mistaken for a precisely preserved seating plan: even the exact site of the medieval Law Rock remains debated.

The assembly was also a gathering place for traders, workers and people looking for news or opportunities. It brought together more than official decision-makers. Political meetings could become important occasions in a dispersed rural society's social calendar.

Visitors built temporary booths with turf and stone walls, wooden frames and coverings. Most visible booth remains are from later centuries, built over older positions. An archaeological footprint may record several assemblies rather than one untouched Commonwealth camp.

The 1939 excavation at Stöng exposed a farmhouse with a hall and attached rooms, alongside evidence for a byre and smithy. Domestic life, livestock care and skilled repair occupied related spaces. The modern reconstructed farm is an interpretation based on excavation.

One attached room contained sunken vats and is commonly interpreted as a pantry; another with long trenches has been interpreted as a latrine. Those functional labels are archaeological interpretations, not signs left on medieval doors.

Stöng is often linked to Hekla's 1104 eruption, but environmental research shows continued activity in the wider valley for two centuries afterward. Volcanic ash can date layers; it does not justify saying that an entire region became empty on one day.

The environmental study examined nine soil profiles containing 92 volcanic-ash layers. Combining those layers with evidence of land use allows researchers to test older stories about sudden abandonment. Discoveries can revise a familiar heritage narrative.

The Alþingi decided in 1117 to have laws written down, and recording took place the following winter. The surviving Grágás tradition includes later copies and fragments. Beginning to write a law is not the same event as producing every surviving manuscript.

A mid 1200s Grágás fragment includes inheritance, support of dependents, property and Christian-law provisions. It later survived as reused book-cover material. Family obligations and practical disputes could be preserved on a sheet rescued from a very different job.

Manuscript AM 677 4to, made around 1200, contains Christian works translated from Latin into Icelandic. Its language and abbreviations help scholars study how early written Icelandic worked. Literature included translated teaching as well as the sagas now especially famous.

Hinn góði maður means “The good person.” It begins a passage quoted from AM 677 4to by the Árni Magnússon Institute in modernized spelling. This short Icelandic sample uses Latin letters; it should not be confused with a facsimile reproducing every medieval abbreviation.

ending.text: Agreements in 1262-1264 brought Iceland under the Norwegian king and ended the Commonwealth's independent political arrangement. Farms, assemblies and Icelandic writing continued. The atlas's 1200 endpoint precedes this change and is not the date the Commonwealth fell.
